approachQuestion.prompt:
Match Public Names

Two ASCII strings nameA and nameB represent public names. In each string, discard every character except English letters, and treat uppercase letters as their lowercase counterparts. Return true if the resulting sequences are identical, including their order. If neither contains a letter, they match.

Example 1: nameA="A-ly 7", nameB="aLY!" → true.
Example 2: nameA="Ab", nameB="ba" → false.
Example 3: nameA="123", nameB="!?" → true.

Constraints:
0 ≤ each string length ≤ 200,000. Only ASCII characters occur.
Do not modify either string. A–Z maps directly to a–z; locale rules do not apply.
Return one Boolean. Digits, spaces and punctuation are discarded.

options.text: Scan each original string with its own index. Skip nonletters, compare the next letters after ASCII case conversion, and advance. Accept only if both scans exhaust their letters together.
options.feedback: Skipping implements exactly the discard rule, conversion handles case, and ordered comparisons preserve sequence order.

options.text: Build a separate lowercase-letter-only string for each input, then compare those strings.
options.feedback: This implements the rule correctly but stores two removable normalized copies; indices can read the original strings.

options.text: Count lowercase letters in each input after discarding nonletters, then compare the counts.
options.feedback: Equal letter counts do not preserve order. "Ab" and "ba" must differ, but their counts agree.

options.text: Lowercase both original strings and compare them without removing anything.
options.feedback: Discarded characters must not affect equality. "A-" and "a" match, but this method rejects them.

feedback.reason: Filtering and lowercasing preserve the order of the remaining letters.
details: Advance separate indices through both originals. Ignore nonletters, compare lowercase forms of the next available letters, and require joint exhaustion.

Filtering and lowercasing preserve the order of the remaining letters. Equal letter counts cannot establish normalized sequence equality. Scan discarded trailing characters too before deciding both sides are exhausted; a name containing only ignored characters has an empty normalized sequence.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For the fixed method “Skip Nonletters and Compare”, choose the tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair. Let N be the sum of both original lengths. Use a tight worst-case bound valid when N=0. ASCII tests, case conversion and indexed character reads cost constant time. No copies, hashing or recursion are used. Include helper indices and stack; exclude input and Boolean output.
constraints: 0 ≤ each string length ≤ 200,000. Only ASCII characters occur.
Do not modify either string. A–Z maps directly to a–z; locale rules do not apply.
Return one Boolean. Digits, spaces and punctuation are discarded.

feedback.reason: Indices advance across originals without allocating normalized copies.
details: Each index advances through its original at most once, including discarded characters. Only two indices and fixed character state are retained. Entire inputs can require inspection even when they contain no letters.
The option “O(N + 1) time, O(1) auxiliary space.”: All original characters can be visited, without normalized copies.
The option “O(N + 1) time, O(N + 1) auxiliary space.”: Normalized copies would consume this space, but the fixed method reads originals.
The option “O(1) time, O(1) auxiliary space.”: Discarded suffixes may require scanning, so work is not constant.
The option “O((N + 1)²) time, O(1) auxiliary space.”: No prefix is rescanned as indices only advance.
